title: swiss back door coco fix looks misguided 2026 09 02
author: Liam Proud
text:
LONDON, Sept 2 (Reuters Breakingviews) - Lawmakers in Switzerland are putting the "concern" into "going concern". A parliamentary committee, which has been deliberating the government's proposed stricter capital rules for $170 billion UBS (UBSG.S)
, opens new tab
, is pushing
, opens new tab
 for reforms to additional Tier 1 (AT1) securities, also known as contingent convertible bonds or CoCos. This form of hybrid ​debt, which became controversial for its role in the emergency rescue of Credit Suisse, would become far more important if the lawmakers get their way. Yet the ‌proposed changes make little sense.
UBS's capital requirements are the subject of an intense political debate in the small Alpine country. On one side is the government, whose Finance Minister Karin Keller-Sutter wants the lender to fully back its foreign subsidiaries with common equity Tier 1 (CET1), the purest form of bank capital, raising its requirement by around $20 billion. On the other side of the debate are some lawmakers in parliament, who seem ​to agree with UBS that the government's plan would undermine competitiveness. On Monday, a committee of Switzerland's upper house proposed that the bank could instead use a ​50-50 split of CET1 and cheaper AT1 debt, which are intended to convert into equity while a troubled bank is still a going ⁠concern.
For UBS, this would be far more palatable, even though the committee also wants to make the new AT1 bonds better at absorbing losses, and hence more expensive than current ​bonds. The bank reckons
, opens new tab
 it might have to issue some $13 billion of extra AT1 securities under the plan. This could cost almost $1 billion a year, assuming a very conservative interest rate ​of 8%, which compares with a 6.4% weighted average yield for the bank's outstanding AT1s. All else equal, the extra cost would dilute the bank's return on tangible equity by about 1 percentage point, according to Breakingviews calculations based on analysts' 2028 forecasts. For comparison, the Keller-Sutter plan might reduce the return by almost 4 percentage points, RBC analysts estimate.
Yet the proposed AT1 tweaks raise questions that extend beyond UBS. ​Since Credit Suisse failed in 2023, regulators and governments have been mulling changes to make sure that CoCos can stabilise a bank before the point of no return. One general ​idea is to bring forward the so-called trigger point, or the minimum CET1 level at which a bank converts the AT1s into equity. This trigger is often around 7% in Britain and Switzerland. ‌The parliamentary committee ⁠could effectively bring in an 11% trigger, by linking it to UBS's regulatory minimum CET1 requirement. If a bank's common equity falls below that level, the proposals state that it would have to cease coupons to conserve capital, and eventually convert the bonds into equity.
There are two issues. First, having an idiosyncratic Swiss regime could make the market more complicated for investors, potentially increasing the costs of the instruments. Second, it's not clear that having a slightly higher trigger point would change much. Credit Suisse failed with a CET1 ratio of 14%, ​well above its minimum requirements. By the ​time a bank gets anywhere near hitting ⁠its balance-sheet buffers, depositors and other creditors have probably already fled.
The political process has many twists and turns ahead for UBS. But the one thing that's clear is that the proposed AT1 tweaks may not avoid the mistakes of the past.
